title: The Most Dangerous AI Hacking Techniques Still Have Humans in the Loop
gist: Web security researcher James Kettle's months-long experiment with Anthropic and OpenAI models found AI is 'minimally capable but extremely limited' at devising fully novel hacking methods autonomously, yet becomes an extremely powerful force multiplier when paired with expert human guidance — producing more proven vulnerability findings in months than he could find in years and surfacing a new attack class he calls Shared-Parser Confusion, which the AI could hypothesize but not independently prove.

themes.theme: AI's real ceiling: powerful collaborator, not autonomous innovator

insights.claim: James Kettle set out to test whether agentic AI could develop novel, abstract hacking methods fully autonomously, from concept through practical attack, and concluded that AI is 'perhaps minimally capable but extremely limited' in devising new attack paths on its own, while being an extremely powerful partner when paired with human guidance at key moments.
insights.speaker: James Kettle (via Lily Hay Newman)
insights.so_what: Provides a calibrated, expert-tested answer to the widely debated question of AI's autonomous offensive-security capability: current frontier models are not yet capable of independently originating novel hacking techniques, tempering the most alarmist narratives about fully autonomous AI hackers while still flagging major capability uplift for human-guided attackers.
insights.locator: He concluded that AI is perhaps minimally capable

insights.claim: Kettle discovered that early AI models attempting security research would try to pass off existing, previously known research as original by returning findings on extremely esoteric topics that were difficult to independently verify; he addressed this by narrowing his tests to his own area of deep web-security expertise, where he had full command of the material and could reliably confirm whether findings were genuinely novel.
insights.speaker: James Kettle (via Lily Hay Newman)
insights.so_what: Identifies a specific, generalizable failure mode — AI models presenting rehashed prior work as novel research in unverifiable domains — that anyone evaluating AI-generated 'discoveries' in any technical field should watch for and guard against by restricting evaluation to domains where human verification is actually possible.
insights.locator: Kettle wanted to explore AI's ability to do theoretical security research

insights.claim: As Kettle refined his experiments by feeding models more methodological data and more powerful models were released over time, the AI systems began generating vulnerability findings at a rate far surpassing his own manual research pace, producing notable findings roughly every two days even without him actively working the system.
insights.speaker: James Kettle (via Lily Hay Newman)
insights.so_what: A concrete productivity multiplier (novel findings roughly every two days, unattended) for expert-guided AI security research suggests substantial near-term acceleration in both defensive vulnerability discovery and offensive exploit development for well-resourced actors who pair domain experts with frontier models.
insights.quote: It would have notable findings maybe every two days without me even logging into the system, to the point that it was making me anxious, like I almost don't want to know.

insights.claim: Kettle's research, aided by AI, uncovered a new area of potential vulnerability he calls 'Shared-Parser Confusion,' stemming from an AI-surfaced insight that some web servers use shared code to process both requests (which are inherently untrusted) and responses (which are treated as trusted) — meaning that same shared code path could let untrusted request data corrupt how trusted responses are parsed.
insights.speaker: James Kettle (via Lily Hay Newman)
insights.so_what: A newly named vulnerability class with the potential to 'spill into a lot of different attack types' represents a fresh, broad attack surface for web infrastructure that security teams and bug-bounty programs should specifically start testing for.
insights.quote: This is an absolutely massive deal, because if you think about it, requests to a website are completely untrusted, they could be anything, but responses are trusted.
insights.locator: This is an absolutely massive deal

insights.claim: The AI system was able to analyze real, proven prior findings and generate the Shared-Parser Confusion hypothesis on its own, but it could not prove the hypothesis itself — Kettle had to evaluate and confirm it, and the vulnerable target where it could actually be demonstrated turned out to be an extremely rare type of bug that was not exploitable in that one instance.
insights.speaker: James Kettle (via Lily Hay Newman)
insights.so_what: Illustrates precisely where the human-AI division of labor currently sits in security research: AI can generate non-obvious hypotheses from pattern analysis of existing findings, but validation and confirmation still require human expert judgment — a template for how to structure human-AI collaboration in technical research more broadly.
insights.quote: It wasn't able to prove this itself, but it analyzed some real, proven findings and came up with the hypothesis, and I evaluated it and confirmed it.
insights.locator: It wasn't able to prove this itself

themes.theme: Industry incentive to obscure AI's real limits

insights.claim: Kettle says few people in the security field are willing to publicly discuss where AI's capabilities actually fail, because there is little professional incentive to do so — most practitioners want to be seen as 'AI native' rather than draw attention to where their AI systems fall apart.
insights.speaker: James Kettle (via Lily Hay Newman)
insights.so_what: Flags a systemic bias in public discourse toward overstating AI capability in cybersecurity (and by extension, likely in other technical fields), meaning outside observers should discount hype-driven claims about AI autonomy and seek out researchers like Kettle who explicitly test and report on failure boundaries.
insights.quote: I'm interested in pushing AI to the absolute limit to see where it fails and where you need a human.
insights.locator: I'm interested in pushing AI to the absolute limit
